opus-5.5.text:
I think it could play a really central role, and honestly I think it's one of the most underappreciated areas of research right now.

If you look at the history of arms control, with nuclear weapons for example, the treaties that actually worked were the ones where countries could check that the other side was complying. "Trust but verify," as the saying went. Nobody signs an agreement that constrains their own capabilities if they believe the other party can just cheat in secret and gain a strategic advantage. That's the core problem we face with AI. The US, China, and others are in a competitive dynamic, and each side fears that if they slow down or accept limits, the other won't.

AI is in some ways harder to verify than nuclear weapons. Software can be copied, models can be hidden, training can happen in a data center that looks like any other. But there are also some handles we can grab onto. Frontier AI training currently requires enormous amounts of specialized compute, very particular chips, huge energy consumption, and a concentrated supply chain. That gives us places where we could build verification mechanisms.

So technical research could explore things like hardware-enabled mechanisms on the chips themselves: ways for a chip to attest to what it's being used for, or to cryptographically prove that a certain amount of compute was or wasn't used for a training run, ideally in a privacy-preserving way so countries don't have to reveal their trade secrets or military applications. There's also work on proving properties of a model without revealing its weights, on tracking where chips go, and on auditing data centers.

The important point is that none of this exists at the maturity we'd need today. And if political leaders decide in a few years that they want an agreement, maybe after some scary incident, we don't want them to be told, "Sorry, we have no way to check compliance." We want the technical options to be ready on the shelf. Diplomacy often moves suddenly when the political window opens, and research takes years. So I'd really encourage people with backgrounds in hardware security, cryptography, and computer architecture to consider working on this. It could be the thing that turns international coordination from wishful thinking into something actually feasible.

r001.rationale: It says technical verification could make AI agreements feasible by letting the US, China, and other countries check compliance despite mutual fears of cheating.

r002.rationale: It proposes chip-based attestation and cryptographic proofs of compute use as verification mechanisms, including privacy-preserving approaches.

r003.rationale: It says research is needed and encourages qualified researchers to work on it, but does not argue that governments need to incentivize that research.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it could play a central role, and I want to explain why I've become so focused on it.

When people hear "international AI treaty," the immediate objection is: how would you ever enforce it? With nuclear weapons, we had a physical thing to count — fissile material, enrichment facilities, missiles. You could send inspectors, you could use satellites. The whole arms control architecture of the Cold War was built on the fact that verification was at least technically possible, even if it was hard politically. With AI, people say, it's just software, it's just math, you can't verify anything. And if you can't verify, then no serious country will sign, because they'll assume the other side is cheating.

So the verification problem is actually the bottleneck. It's not that governments don't understand the risks — I've talked with many of them, and the understanding is growing quickly. It's that nobody wants to be the one who tied their own hands while a rival didn't. That's a classic coordination failure, and the way out of a coordination failure is to make defection detectable.

Now, the good news is that I don't think AI is as unverifiable as people assume. The physical layer still exists. Frontier training runs require enormous quantities of specialized chips, concentrated in a small number of data centers, consuming power at a scale that's visible from the grid. That's not nothing. There's a lot of interesting work on hardware-enabled mechanisms — chips that can attest to what workloads they're running, or that can be made to require periodic cryptographic authorization to keep operating, so that if a treaty is violated, you have levers. Some of this is still early, but the components mostly exist; it's more an engineering and standardization problem than a fundamental scientific one.

Then there's the software and model side. Can two parties who don't trust each other agree that a model satisfies some property without one of them revealing their weights? There's progress on that too — things borrowed from cryptography, secure multiparty computation, zero-knowledge proofs, and also simpler approaches like trusted third-party evaluation under strict conditions. And my own research direction, which is about building AI systems that can give you a reliable, calibrated estimate of whether an action or a claim is safe — that's also, in a sense, a verification technology. If you can have an AI "scientist" that is honest about its uncertainty, then it becomes a tool for checking other systems rather than only a source of risk.

What I find encouraging is the analogy with the history of arms control. In the 1950s there were people doing very technical, kind of unglamorous research on seismic detection of nuclear tests. At the time, this looked like a niche geophysics problem. But without it, the test ban treaties would never have been possible. The technical work created the political possibility. I think we're at that moment with AI. If researchers can demonstrate, credibly, that you can detect large unauthorized training runs, or that you can confirm compute is being used within agreed limits without exposing secrets, then suddenly a treaty goes from utopian to something diplomats can actually draft.

And I'd add one more thing. Verification research is also unusually attractive because it's something every side has reason to want. Even if you're a country that's worried about falling behind, you still prefer to know what your competitor is doing. So this is research that can get funding and cooperation across geopolitical lines in a way that, say, pausing development cannot. It's where the technical community can give the political world a gift: not a solution to the whole problem, but the thing that makes the rest of the conversation possible.

So I would say to young researchers: this is a place where your technical work can have an outsized effect on whether humanity manages this transition well. It's not the most glamorous part of AI, but it may turn out to be one of the most important.

r001.rationale: It presents technical verification as a way to make defection detectable and says that could make treaties feasible even when countries distrust one another.

r002.rationale: It describes hardware that attests to workloads or requires cryptographic authorization, alongside cryptographic methods for checking model properties, as verification mechanisms.

r003.rationale: It says verification research could attract funding and cooperation and make treaties possible, but does not argue that governments seeking signable treaties need to incentivize that research.

astra-6.text:
I think it could play a very important role, because one of the obstacles to an international agreement is trust. Even if countries agree that they would all be better off with some constraints on developing very powerful AI, each will worry that the others are secretly going ahead. An agreement is much more credible if there are ways to check compliance.

Technical research can help us understand what we could actually verify. Could we verify that a large training run respects an agreed limit? Could we establish that a system underwent the required safety evaluations? And could we do those things without revealing commercial secrets or sensitive national security information? Those are research questions, and the answers could change which agreements are feasible.

Of course, verifying that an evaluation took place is different from proving that an AI system is safe. We should be careful about what the evidence establishes. But we don’t necessarily need perfect verification to make cooperation worthwhile. We need mechanisms that make violations sufficiently difficult to hide, together with political agreements about inspections and consequences.

So I would like to see technical researchers and people working on international governance collaborate much more closely. The technical work can give negotiators concrete options, and the negotiations can tell researchers which verification problems matter most.

r001.rationale: It says verification mechanisms could make international agreements more credible by addressing countries’ concerns that others may secretly violate them.

r002.rationale: It discusses ways to verify compliance, but does not suggest modifying AI software or hardware to improve verification.

r003.rationale: It calls for technical researchers and governance experts to collaborate, but does not argue that governments should incentivize verification research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could play a very important role, because one of the obstacles to an international agreement is trust. Even if governments agree that some forms of AI development would be too dangerous, they will worry that others are secretly continuing. So we need ways to verify compliance that don’t depend only on promises.

For example, could we verify that a very large training run has taken place, or that it has respected certain constraints? Could we check that required safety evaluations were actually performed? And could we do that without revealing all of a company’s intellectual property, or sensitive information about a country’s activities? Those are technical research questions, and better answers could make agreements more feasible politically.

Of course, verifying how much computation was used is different from verifying that a system is safe. We shouldn’t confuse the two. But even partial verification could be useful if it makes violations harder to hide and gives countries more confidence that others are following the same rules.

So I wouldn’t wait until we have a treaty to do this research. The technical tools can help determine what commitments we can realistically ask countries to make.

r001.rationale: It says technical methods for verifying compliance could build trust between governments and make international agreements more feasible.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of verification questions but does not suggest modifying AI software or hardware to enable reliable verification.

r003.rationale: It recommends doing verification research before a treaty, but does not argue that governments need to incentivize that research.
